title: Positioning
summary: CSS position controls how a box is placed. Some choices use the normal page order, and others place a box more freely.
introduction: CSS position controls how a box is placed. Some choices use the normal page order, and others place a box more freely. Try each choice on a small box. Learn what the box uses as its starting point before changing top or left.
learningObjectives: Explain how static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky differ
Choose the correct containing block with position: relative on an ancestor
Layer elements with z-index and recognise stacking contexts

blocks.text: Every element starts with `position: static`: it sits where normal flow puts it, and the offset properties `top`, `right`, `bottom` and `left` (or the `inset` shorthand) have no effect on it. Writing `top: 20px` and seeing nothing happen almost always means the element is still static. The four other values change what the offsets are measured from.
relative: nudge without disturbing the flow

A relatively positioned element is offset from *its own normal position*, and the space it would have occupied stays reserved, so nothing else moves. Small nudges are one use; the more important one is that a relatively positioned element becomes the **containing block** for absolutely positioned descendants, as the next section shows.

Sample heading

The paragraph does not move up: the heading's original space is still reserved.

blocks.text: absolute: taken out of the flow

An absolutely positioned element is removed from normal flow: it takes no space, and other elements are laid out as if it did not exist. Its offsets are measured from the nearest ancestor whose `position` is anything other than `static`; if there is none, from the initial containing block, which is the page. That is why the recipe for a badge in the corner of a card is two declarations: `position: relative` on the card (to make it the reference) and `position: absolute` on the badge.

blocks.text: The `inset` shorthand sets all four offsets at once (`inset: 0` stretches the element over its whole containing block, a common overlay trick). Setting both `left` and `right` without a width also stretches it horizontally.

`position: fixed` works like `absolute` but the reference is the viewport, so the element stays put while the page scrolls: cookie banners, chat buttons, persistent headers. It takes no space either, so add padding to the `body` if content must not end up hidden underneath it. One caveat: if an ancestor has a `transform`, `filter` or `perspective`, that ancestor becomes the containing block and the element is no longer fixed to the viewport.

blocks.text: sticky: in the flow until it reaches a threshold

A sticky element behaves like a relative one, keeping its place and its space, until the nearest scrolling ancestor scrolls it to the offset you set, typically `top: 0`. From then on it stays at that offset, but only while its *parent* is on screen: when the parent scrolls away, the sticky element goes with it. Section headings in a long list are the classic use.

blocks.title: When sticky silently does nothing
blocks.text: Two mistakes make `position: sticky` look unsupported. The first is forgetting the threshold: without `top` (or another offset) there is nothing to stick to. The second is an ancestor with `overflow: hidden`, `auto` or `scroll` that has no fixed height: it becomes the scrolling ancestor, and since it never scrolls, the element never sticks. Check both before blaming the browser.

Positioned elements paint on top of normal flow, and `z-index` orders positioned elements (and flex or grid items) among themselves: a higher integer is closer to the viewer. The catch is that `z-index` is only compared between elements in the same **stacking context**. A new context is created by a positioned element with a `z-index` other than `auto`, and also by `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `position: fixed` or `sticky`, among others. Once an element is inside a context, no `z-index` value can lift it above an element that sits above that whole context, which explains the classic mystery of a `z-index: 9999` dropdown hiding behind a `z-index: 1` header: the dropdown's parent created a context that is below the header.

blocks.title: Positioning is not layout
blocks.text: Use positioning for things that overlap or stick: badges, tooltips, dropdowns, banners, headers. For arranging content side by side or in columns, reach for [Flexbox](/tutorials/css/flexbox) and [Grid](/tutorials/css/grid), which keep elements in the flow and adapt to their content.

questions.question: An element with `position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0;` is placed in the top-right corner of what?
questions.explanation: Absolute positioning uses the nearest ancestor whose position is not static as its reference. Only when no such ancestor exists does it fall back to the page.
options: The nearest ancestor whose `position` is not `static`, otherwise the page

questions.question: `position: relative` removes the element from normal flow so other elements fill its space.
questions.explanation: Relative positioning offsets the element visually but keeps its original space reserved. Only `absolute` and `fixed` remove an element from the flow.
